proposed_node.title: Cardiolipin and respiratory supercomplex stability
proposed_node.canonical_question: What is the role of cardiolipin in stabilising the respiratory supercomplexes?
proposed_node.summary: Cardiolipin is a dimeric phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane that acts as molecular glue at the contact interfaces between Complexes I, III, and IV. It stabilises these respirasomes, supports electron channelling efficiency, and its loss — as in Barth syndrome — destabilises supercomplexes and impairs ATP production.

sections.heading: What are respiratory supercomplexes?
sections.body: The four protein complexes of the electron transport chain (Complex I, II, III, and IV) can exist as individual units floating in the inner mitochondrial membrane, but they can also associate into larger assemblies called supercomplexes or respirasomes. The most prominent supercomplex contains one copy of Complex I, two copies of Complex III, and one or two copies of Complex IV. These assemblies are not static scaffolds — they are held together largely by lipid interactions, and cardiolipin is the most important of those lipids.

sections.heading: Cardiolipin: a phospholipid built for the job
sections.body: Cardiolipin (CL) is structurally unusual. Where a typical membrane phospholipid has one glycerol head group, two acyl chains, and one phosphate, cardiolipin has two phosphate groups bridged by a central glycerol, giving it four acyl chains and a distinctly wedge-like shape. This geometry means cardiolipin fits snugly into the concave contact zones between neighbouring protein complexes. Cardiolipin is found almost exclusively in the inner mitochondrial membrane and in bacterial plasma membranes — consistent with the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria — and it makes up about 15 to 20 percent of the lipids in that membrane.

sections.heading: How cardiolipin stabilises the supercomplex
sections.body: X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy studies have revealed cardiolipin molecules bound at the interface between Complex I and Complex III, and between Complex III and Complex IV, within the supercomplex. Cardiolipin fills hydrophobic gaps at these protein-protein contact surfaces, reducing the energetic cost of keeping the complexes together. It also bridges subunits within each individual complex — for example, it stabilises the association of the peripheral arm of Complex I with the membrane arm. Removing cardiolipin, either enzymatically or through genetic mutation, causes the supercomplex to dissociate into its constituent complexes.

sections.heading: Why does supercomplex formation matter for ATP production?
sections.body: Grouping the complexes together is thought to provide two key advantages. First, it supports substrate channelling: the mobile electron carriers ubiquinol and cytochrome c have shorter distances to travel between complexes when those complexes are in direct contact, which speeds up electron flux. Second, tighter coupling reduces the chance that electrons leak to molecular oxygen before reaching Complex IV, which lowers the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). In effect, cardiolipin-stabilised supercomplexes make the electron transport chain both faster and safer.

sections.heading: Barth syndrome: what happens when cardiolipin is abnormal
sections.body: The importance of cardiolipin is illustrated by Barth syndrome, a rare X-linked condition caused by mutations in the gene encoding tafazzin, an enzyme that remodels the acyl chains of cardiolipin after its initial synthesis. Without functional tafazzin, cells accumulate immature cardiolipin and a related lipid called monolysocardiolipin. Respiratory supercomplexes become unstable, individual complexes lose activity, and the inner mitochondrial membrane architecture is disrupted. Patients develop cardiomyopathy, skeletal muscle weakness, and growth delay — all tissues with high energy demand, which shows how directly supercomplex stability depends on correct cardiolipin composition.

sections.heading: Connection to the main lesson
sections.body: The electron transport chain was introduced as the machinery that uses electrons from NADH and FADH2 to pump protons and ultimately drive ATP synthesis. Cardiolipin and supercomplex organisation sit one level deeper: they explain why the chain works as efficiently as it does. The inner mitochondrial membrane is not just a passive barrier; its lipid composition actively shapes how the protein complexes are arranged and how well electrons flow from one complex to the next. This is a good example of how membrane structure and protein function are inseparable in cell biology.

rendering.explanation: The electron transport chain is not just a row of isolated proteins floating randomly in the membrane. Complexes I, III, and IV can snap together into a larger assembly called a supercomplex or respirasome. The molecular glue that holds them together is a lipid called cardiolipin. Cardiolipin is unusual because it has four fatty acid tails and two phosphate groups rather than the two tails and one phosphate of a typical membrane lipid. This shape lets it wedge into the gaps between the complexes at their contact zones, holding the assembly stable. When cardiolipin is present and correctly shaped, electrons can hop between complexes quickly and with fewer harmful side-reactions. When cardiolipin is missing or malformed — as happens in a condition called Barth syndrome, caused by a mutation in the enzyme that trims cardiolipin's fatty acid chains — the supercomplexes fall apart, the chain becomes less efficient, and cells in energy-hungry tissues like the heart struggle to keep up. So cardiolipin is not just a structural filler; it is a key regulator of how well the respiratory chain performs.
